disease_info: Anorexia nervosa is an eating disorder characterized by a persistent restriction of energy intake leading to significantly low body weight, an intense fear of gaining weight or becoming fat, and a disturbance in the way one’s body weight or shape is experienced. Patients often exhibit rigid dietary rules, overvaluation of thinness, and may deny the seriousness of their low weight despite medical compromise. Onset is most common in adolescence or young adulthood but can appear or recur later in life, often around stressful transitions or identity challenges, and the course can be chronic, relapsing, or episodic. It is distinguished from other eating disorders by the underweight status and primary focus on restriction rather than recurrent binge eating or overt compensatory behaviors like vomiting, although some individuals may also misuse exercise or other methods to influence weight.

narrative.stressor: Tonya’s eating issues began to intensify when she started taking on larger, higher‑end residential projects and mentoring apprentices while studying for her certified lead‑painter credential. Long days on job sites, pressure to keep projects on tight timelines, and the physical demands of climbing ladders and hauling materials led her to focus increasingly on staying “lean and light” for work, which gradually shifted from a casual goal into a rigid preoccupation with controlling what she ate. As she began drafting business plans for her own sustainable finish company, the stress of proving herself in a male‑dominated trade and maintaining a certain image in front of eco‑conscious clients further reinforced her restrictive habits, even as friends noticed she was shrinking and skipping shared meals after weekend concerts or Habitat builds. She finally agreed to see a psychiatrist after nearly fainting on a ladder at a client’s home, which forced her to cancel jobs and scared both her apprentices and her parents, who insisted she get evaluated when they realized how much weight she had lost.
narrative.chief_complaint: I’ve gotten so strict about what and how much I eat that I’m barely eating at all and it’s starting to interfere with my work on job sites.

narrative.stressor: Steven’s weight and eating concerns became more pronounced over several years as he tried to juggle long hours at the shop, his community basketball league, and being a present husband and father, all while sketching plans to open a high‑performance EV repair business. When his teenage daughter began struggling with her own body image and social media pressures, he became hyper‑focused on being a “healthy role model,” which gradually morphed into a rigid drive to be as lean and fit as possible, despite his already slim build. Family dinners that used to center on his barbecue became tense as he increasingly avoided food he once enjoyed, and his wife noticed him growing more withdrawn and irritable when relatives commented on how thin he looked at gatherings and church events. The situation came to a head after his daughter confided to the school counselor about her worries that her dad was “barely eating and always talking about not getting fat,” leading the counselor to recommend that the whole family seek support; Steven reluctantly agreed to a psychiatric evaluation when his wife confronted him with the extent of his weight loss and how it was affecting their home life.
narrative.chief_complaint: I can’t shake this fear of putting on weight, so I keep cutting back on what I eat even though my family says I’m already too thin.

narrative.stressor: Yen’s longstanding perfectionism around her craft intensified as she approached her 60s and began thinking about scaling back on heavy carpentry work and transitioning more into design and mentoring. The prospect of aging out of the physically demanding aspects of the trade, combined with subtle ageist comments on job sites and at woodworking meet‑ups, led her to focus more and more on maintaining a youthful, agile image that she felt matched her reputation as a meticulous artisan. Over several years, she quietly lost weight while telling herself it was just the result of “eating cleaner” and doing more tai chi and cycling, even as colleagues and family expressed concern and she began needing to sit down more often during long days in the workshop. She finally sought psychiatric care at the urging of her primary care physician, who, after seeing her for fatigue and irregular lab results, recommended a mental health evaluation when Yen minimized her low weight and could not see why others were so worried about how thin she had become.
narrative.chief_complaint: Everyone keeps telling me I’m too thin and need to gain weight, but I honestly don’t see what the big problem is with my size right now.
